title: Push Deploys vs GitOps: Who’s Really in Charge? 🔁
ig_caption:
3AM “hotfix” into prod… then what? Push vs GitOps explained 🔥

• Push deploys: you run an update straight into the cluster.
• Someone edits prod by hand (because it’s 3AM)… and the real desired state quietly diverges.
• Next redeploy/hotfix workflow wipes the change → drift goes unnoticed until an outage or mismatch appears.
• GitOps: the desired state lives in Git, and the cluster continuously reconciles to match it.
• Time to notice: “Git = cluster” — if prod changes outside the workflow, reconciliation flags the drift and restores correctness.
• Result: fewer surprises, auditable changes, and safer recovery when incidents happen.

Practical takeaway: Treat Git as your source of truth and route all production changes through the same declarative pipeline—manual prod edits should be either impossible or immediately reconciled.

What’s more dangerous in your org: silent drift (Push) or slow detection/feedback (naive GitOps)—and how do you measure it?

fb_caption:
Push Deploys vs GitOps is less about tools and more about where “truth” lives.

With push-based deployments, the release system pushes desired versions into a target cluster. If a human makes an emergency modification in production (especially common during 3AM incidents), that change becomes an untracked, out-of-band mutation. Unless the platform has strong drift detection and guardrails, the organization may not notice until the next deployment, rollback, or redeploy overwrites the manual change—leading to the exact failure mode your animation calls out: “0 manual changes… hotfix wiped.”

GitOps flips the model:
- Git is the source of truth for desired state.
- Controllers continuously reconcile the cluster to match what’s declared in Git.
- Any out-of-band change becomes drift and is either corrected or clearly surfaced.

Architectural trade-offs:
- Resilience & recovery: GitOps improves incident recovery because the system can deterministically converge back to the last known-good desired state.
- Scalability & governance: With Git as the workflow boundary, you get consistent review/audit, easier rollbacks, and standardized promotion between environments.
- Operational overhead: GitOps introduces a reconciliation loop and requires disciplined declarative configuration, but the long-term payoff is fewer “mystery states.”

Production best practice:
Use declarative state + continuous reconciliation, and restrict or rapidly neutralize manual production edits. Combine GitOps with observability (drift alerts, reconciliation events) so you detect divergence quickly and restore automatically.

Question for the community: In your environment, what signals convince you that “Git = cluster” is actually being enforced—metrics, alerts, or incidents?
threads_caption: Push deploys can hide drift when humans hotfix prod. GitOps reconciles back to “Git = cluster” and makes drift visible. Which failure mode has hurt you more: silent overwrite or delayed detection? 🔁
